case_study_insert.main_stem: Wellcare Home Services (WHC) is a private limited company in the domestic care and cleaning services sector, employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2012 by Amina Yusuf, the business produces home care kit units for elderly clients and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. WHC plans to invest $560,000 in a new automated kit-packing centre with biodegradable packaging, financed by a $320,000 six-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $20 a unit and a selling price of $38, and currently produces 22,000 units a year. WHC faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and more clients report missing or damaged items in delivered kits.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2025: WHC packed 4,100 home care kits last quarter with a packing-error rate of 2.4%, down from 3.9% a year ago. Complaints about missing items fell from 26 to 8 per month. Average delivery time is 2.9 days. A survey of 420 clients found that 74% would pay up to $1.20 more for kits in biodegradable packaging, and 63% check packaging when choosing a home-care supplier.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Wellcare Home Services for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.9%. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.10 to $13.82 per hour from April 2027. (3) Packaging and cleaning-material input costs have risen 10.2% year-on-year, consumer-services inflation is 6.8%, and household spending on home-care services grew 3.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: WHC is funding part of its $560,000 kit-packing centre with a $320,000 six-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for WHC of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charges or repayments, so the $240,000 provided internally is cheaper than the $320,000 six-year bank loan. The cash kept can cover the $270,000 a year fixed costs while labour turnover and the 2.4% packing-error rate disrupt the 4,100 kits packed last quarter, protecting the $38 selling price and the cash needed to serve 36 staff.

Point 2: Using internal money keeps control with Amina Yusuf and the existing owners, since no lender can set conditions on how the biodegradable-packaging centre is run or which clients are served. With a flat structure and democratic leadership, that independence suits WHC; if demand falls below 22,000 kits there is no loan to reschedule and no security at risk, so the business can respond quickly to the 26-to-8 fall in missing-item complaints.

This protects the cash needed to replace packing equipment while errors are investigated, and leaves Amina Yusuf free to change the client mix without consulting a lender.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to WHC and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: WHC is launching its new biodegradable-packaged home care kits. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should WHC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV advert could build awareness of biodegradable kits among elderly clients and their families, supporting the $560,000 centre. However, airtime and production are very costly for a 36-employee business already committing to a $320,000 loan, and many viewers are not buyers of home-care kits, so much of the budget would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is cheap and can reach clients near WHC, where the 2.9-day delivery time is strongest, making it useful for a short launch message. Its weakness is narrow reach: clients are spread more widely, so local listeners alone are unlikely to create the 22,000-unit volume needed to cover $270,000 fixed costs.

Social media influencer marketing: Caregiver and family-wellbeing influencers can show the biodegradable packaging and kit contents directly to the people who choose home-care supplies, with measurable engagement and low cost per contact. It lets WHC use the survey evidence that 74% of 420 clients would pay $1.20 more for biodegradable kits and 63% check packaging, turning Appendix 1 into a precise message.

Recommendation: WHC should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact client group in the research, is far cheaper than television and wider than local radio, and supports the $1.20 premium needed after the 10.2% input-cost rise. Television is rejected as unaffordable for a $560,000 expansion, and radio is rejected as too geographically narrow for a business targeting 22,000 kits a year.

Influencer posts can also be adjusted quickly if clients raise concerns about the biodegradable packaging, which a fixed television advert cannot do.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to WHC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WHC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed analysis of all three options in the context of WHC with a justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: WHC has rising labour turnover and clients report missing or damaged kit items. Explain two benefits for WHC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its packing team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 36 staff a say in how kits are assembled and checked, so they feel valued and are more likely to stay. That directly addresses the rising labour turnover that is disrupting the 4,100 kits packed each quarter and the flat structure makes it natural for packers to suggest better checking routines for missing items.

Point 2: Consulting the people who fill the kits generates practical ideas for cutting the 2.4% packing-error rate, such as a standard checklist or clearer shelf layout. Greater involvement raises commitment and pride, which helps reduce the complaints that fell from 26 to 8 per month, so quality improves at source while the new $560,000 centre is introduced and the 2.9-day delivery time is protected.

The flat structure supports this because there are few layers to block suggestions, so a packer's idea for a clearer kit checklist can be tried the same week, raising both motivation and the accuracy of the 4,100 kits.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to WHC's turnover, packing errors and delivery performance.

questions.question_text: WHC wants to reduce labour turnover and the 2.4% packing-error rate. Consider introducing job enrichment or offering a performance-related bonus for error-free kits. Which should WHC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Job enrichment: Giving packers fuller responsibility for a whole kit, including the final quality check, makes the work more meaningful and can reduce labour turnover. Staff develop a clearer sense of ownership over the 4,100 kits, which helps catch missing items and fits the democratic, flat structure. It requires careful redesign and training, and results in lower packing errors may take time to appear.

Performance-related bonus: Paying extra for kits that pass the final check creates an immediate financial incentive and could build on the fall in complaints from 26 to 8 per month. It is simple to operate if the 2.4% error data are recorded, but it costs cash each period, may encourage staff to conceal mistakes to qualify, and does not tackle the repetitive work that drives turnover.

Decision: WHC should introduce job enrichment. It addresses the root cause of turnover by making packing more satisfying, uses the existing democratic leadership, and improves quality ownership without a recurring cash cost while the $560,000 centre is funded. The bonus is rejected because it rewards the outcome without changing the boring work, needs reliable measurement and adds expense; it can be considered later if error rates remain high.

Cost matters too: WHC is funding $240,000 of the $560,000 centre from retained profit, and a recurring bonus would compete with that commitment and with the $270,000 fixed costs. Job enrichment uses the existing democratic style and builds multi-skilled staff who can cover for absent colleagues, which is more valuable than a payment that stops rewarding behaviour once it ends. The bonus is rejected for that reason and because it does not change the routine that drives turnover.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two approaches with limited application to WHC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of WHC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluation of both approaches with a justified decision covering motivation, cost and measurement, explaining why the alternative is rejected.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WHC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $270,000 ÷ ($38 − $20) = $270,000 ÷ $18 = 15,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 15,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $38 − $20 = $18. Answer: contribution per unit is $18.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WHC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 15,000-unit break-even output with 22,000 kits produced: the margin of safety is 7,000 units, showing the cushion against rising labour turnover and client complaints before a loss.
2. Use the $18 contribution per unit to test the $1.20 premium from the survey: raising the $38 price to $39.20 would lift contribution to $19.20, so about 14,063 kits would cover $270,000 fixed costs, guiding the pricing decision.
3. Average total cost is about $32.27 a kit ($270,000 ÷ 22,000 = $12.27 plus $20) against the $38 price, giving a benchmark for the new packing centre and a floor for client quotes.
4. Labour productivity is about 611 units per worker (22,000 ÷ 36); tracking it each quarter shows whether packing errors and turnover are eroding efficiency and whether the $560,000 centre is delivering its intended gain.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 15,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $18 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 7,000 units against 22,000 units output; pricing test of the $1.20 premium against $270,000 fixed costs; average total cost of about $32.27 against the $38 price; and labour productivity of about 611 units per worker to monitor turnover and packing errors.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WHC's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has WHC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 14.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.5%

Detailed workings:
2024: revenue 700, cost of sales 420, gross profit 280; 2025: revenue 840, cost of sales 462, gross profit 378. Operating profit rose from 84 to 126 and capital employed from 600 to 720. Interest payable moved from 16 to 20.

Evaluation: All three measures point to an improved position. The trading margin rose from 40.0% to 45.0% because cost of sales grew more slowly than revenue, so each dollar of client sales left more gross profit despite the 2.4% packing-error rate. The operating margin improved from 12.0% to 15.0%, showing the $270,000 fixed costs were absorbed more efficiently as the 22,000-kit target neared. Return on capital rose from 14.0% to 17.5% even with a larger capital base, a good sign before the $560,000 centre is added.

Conclusion: WHC's financial position has improved. Higher trading margin, operating margin and return on capital all support the view that the business is more profitable and uses its capital better, so it is better placed to service the $320,000 bank loan. The reservations are rising interest payable from 16 to 20 and the 10.2% rise in packaging costs, which make the $1.20 premium important to secure.

Gross profit rising from 280 to 378 is encouraging because it was achieved while the business dealt with rising labour turnover and missing-item complaints, so the improvement is likely to be sustainable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of margin and capital trends and a justified conclusion on whether WHC's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WHC of introducing biodegradable packaging for its home care kits.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey shows 74% of 420 clients would pay up to $1.20 more for kits in biodegradable packaging and 63% check packaging when choosing a supplier, so WHC can lift the $18 contribution per unit and protect the improved trading margin shown in Appendix 2 against the 10.2% rise in packaging and cleaning-material costs. It also fits the $560,000 centre's green positioning and can help win elderly-care clients.

Disadvantage: Biodegradable materials may cost more or protect contents less well than standard packaging, so the $20 variable cost per unit could rise and squeeze contribution if the full $1.20 premium is not accepted. Weaker packaging could also worsen the 2.4% packing-error rate and the missing-item complaints that fell from 26 to 8 per month, harming client trust while labour turnover is rising.

WHC should also confirm that the new materials do not slow the 2.9-day delivery time to elderly clients.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to WHC's research, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.9%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase to $13.82 and the 10.2% rise in packaging and cleaning-material input costs will affect WHC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.9%): The increase is 0.9 percentage points, so if the $320,000 six-year bank loan is variable-rate the extra cost is 0.009 × $320,000 = $2,880 a year. That is small beside $270,000 fixed costs and zero if the loan is fixed, so WHC can largely remove this risk by fixing the rate. It is the least serious of the three changes.

Minimum wage rise (5.5% to $13.82): The insert does not state hours worked or existing pay for the 36 staff, so an exact annual wage total cannot be invented. The defensible judgement is that the whole payroll becomes dearer while output must stay near 22,000 kits to cover $270,000 fixed costs; with labour turnover already rising, extra recruitment and training costs may add to the pressure on unit labour cost.

Packaging and material rise (10.2%): As an explicitly labelled upper bound, if the entire $20 variable cost were exposed, 0.102 × $20 = $2.04 per kit, or $44,880 a year at 22,000 units, reducing contribution from $18 to about $15.96. Even a smaller pass-through matters on every kit, although the 74% of clients who might accept a $1.20 premium gives WHC some scope to recover it.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in packaging and cleaning-material costs has the greatest impact because it applies to all 22,000 kits and directly reduces the $18 contribution that supports the $560,000 centre. The interest rise is only $2,880 a year and can be fixed, and the wage effect is spread across payroll and cannot be quantified from the insert, so neither threatens margin as quickly.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to WHC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on WHC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a justified greatest-impact judgment with reasons for rejecting the other two.
